title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the paragraph that argues both ways, and who arranged what

questions.prompt: Read this note, left on the table of a rented flat. "We are glad you have chosen our flat for the fortnight. The key to the roof terrace and the timetable of the number 4 bus are in the drawer of this desk. The neighbour on the ground floor keeps a spare key, so ring her bell if the door ever locks behind you." Who is the audience, and what is the occasion?

options.text: The cleaning staff, at the end of every fortnight.
The neighbour downstairs, before the tenants come.
The owner's own family, at the very end of the summer season.
The people renting the flat, on the day they arrive.

questions.explanation: The three marks of a situation are all in the note. We stands for the owners, you stands for whoever has taken the flat, and everything the note hands over — a key, a bus timetable, a bell to ring — is what you need on the first day and not on the last: the audience is "The people renting the flat, on the day they arrive." "The neighbour downstairs, before the tenants come." reads the note as addressed to the person it merely mentions in the third person, her. "The cleaning staff, at the end of every fortnight." ignores the welcome in the first line, which nobody writes to a cleaner. "The owner's own family, at the very end of the summer season." reverses the we and the you: the family would not be told where their own roof key lives.

questions.prompt: Only one of these four ways of joining the two halves is not allowed in English. Which one?

options.text: The hall was full, so we sat on the stairs.
The hall was full, we sat on the stairs.
The hall was full. We sat on the stairs.
The hall was full; we sat on the stairs.

questions.explanation: Each half here is a whole sentence, and a comma on its own cannot hold two whole sentences together: "The hall was full, we sat on the stairs." is the join English refuses. The other three all give the comma some help. "The hall was full, so we sat on the stairs." adds a linking word, and so is enough to make one sentence of the two. "The hall was full. We sat on the stairs." closes the first with a full stop and opens the second with a capital, which is always available to you. "The hall was full; we sat on the stairs." uses the semicolon, the mark kept for exactly this — two complete sentences held close together without a linking word.

questions.prompt: Two warnings about the same fuel tank. (1) "A leak here could poison the wells." (2) "A leak here will poison the wells." Which of these is true of the second and not of the first?

options.text: He states it as a conclusion drawn from evidence.
He states it as an order given to the reader.
He states it as no more than a possibility.
He states it as something he expects to happen.

questions.explanation: could says a thing is possible and leaves the reader free to weigh it; will says the writer expects it, so the second warning is a prediction rather than a risk — "He states it as something he expects to happen." "He states it as no more than a possibility." describes could, that is the first warning and not the second. "He states it as a conclusion drawn from evidence." is the work of must: the streets are wet, it must have rained. "He states it as an order given to the reader." belongs to an imperative or to a modal of obligation, and neither of these two sentences tells anybody to do anything. The price of will is that a reader who does not already share the prediction stops reading there, which is why an argument about the future usually hedges.

questions.prompt: Two lines from the same page, both built on have + object + past participle. (1) "Nabil had his flat repainted while he was away." (2) "Nabil had his windscreen cracked by a stone on the motorway." What separates them?

options.text: In the first he arranged the work; in the second nothing was arranged.
In the first he did the work himself; in the second somebody did it for him.
In the first he is the one who suffers it; in the second he is not.
In the first the work is still to come; in the second it is already over.

questions.explanation: have something done always takes the action off the subject, but it then splits in two, and the meaning of the verb tells you which way: "In the first he arranged the work; in the second nothing was arranged." Nobody arranges to have a windscreen cracked by a stone, so the second line can only be reporting what happened to him. "In the first he did the work himself; in the second somebody did it for him." is the classic misreading: had his flat repainted is exactly what you say when you did not hold the brush. "In the first he is the one who suffers it; in the second he is not." reverses the two. "In the first the work is still to come; in the second it is already over." reads a difference of time where there is none: both are finished.

questions.prompt: These six sentences make one paragraph that argues both sides of a question. Put them back in the order that holds together.

options.text: On the other hand, working through August has a cost that is easy to forget.
This is what separates it from an allowance handed over at the end of every week.
A holiday job gives a student something no lesson can give: a first wage that is entirely his own.
Such a summer leaves him arriving in September more worn out than he was in June.
What is more, an employer who has never met you judges you on what you do rather than on what you say.
While a month behind a counter teaches patience, it also takes away the only weeks of the year in which a tired pupil can do nothing at all.

questions.explanation: Only one sentence points at nothing behind it and carries no connector, so only one can open: the claim that a holiday job gives a first wage of the student's own. This is what separates it must come straight after, because its This and its it both point back at that wage and at nothing else. What is more then adds a second advantage to the same side, and it has to come before the turn, not after it: an addition dropped behind the pivot would promise the reader more good news and hand him a drawback. On the other hand is that pivot, and it needs a first side already built, which the three sentences in front of it have built. While a month behind a counter teaches patience concedes a good point and objects in its main half, which is the first thing said on the new side. Such a summer closes, because Such needs a summer already described, and only the sentence about the weeks taken away has described one. The two backward-pointing sentences, This and Such, are what lock the order: each of them can stand in exactly one place.

questions.prompt: A writer answers the objection that a new medical technique is against nature like this: "People said exactly that about the first heart operations, and nobody says it today." What is he doing?

options.text: He is admitting that the objection is right, and then moving on.
He is claiming that whatever people once refused always turns out to be safe.
He is proving that the new technique is the same thing as a heart operation.
He is showing that this objection has been made before and did not last.

questions.explanation: The sentence attacks the objection's record rather than the technique: "He is showing that this objection has been made before and did not last." That is a narrow claim and a strong one, and it costs a single sentence. "He is proving that the new technique is the same thing as a heart operation." claims far more than the writer does — he never says the two are alike, only that the same argument was once used against something we now accept. "He is claiming that whatever people once refused always turns out to be safe." turns one example into a law, and the word always is what makes it indefensible: some things people refused deserved to be refused. "He is admitting that the objection is right, and then moving on." mistakes a rebuttal for a concession.
